summary:
Forgotten Explorers is an interactive website about the machines humanity has left on the Moon, Mars and across the Solar System. It’s built for students and anyone curious about space.

The centerpiece is the Hardware Locator. It’s a 3D globe of the Moon and Mars that pins landers, rovers, instruments and retroreflectors to their real coordinates, and shows whether each one still works. In the 3D Mars Rover experience, visitors drive a rover across the Martian surface. The 3D Virtual Museum lets them walk through a gallery of real spacecraft and artifacts. The Silent Legacy is a narrated documentary made from NASA archival imagery. Mission pages explain why each machine went, what it discovered, and who built it. Visitors can also follow a timeline, compare international missions, explore the Solar System, and ask questions to NOVA, a built-in AI guide.

The project answers the challenge’s three questions: where these explorers are, why they went, and what they found. Every image is authentic NASA imagery, and every fact links to its source. The site works in five languages and has a Low Data Mode and accessible design. These machines are humanity’s first footprints on other worlds, and the project keeps their stories alive.
details:
What it does

Forgotten Explorers is a free, interactive website about the hardware humanity has left on the Moon, Mars and across the Solar System. It answers three questions: where are these machines, why did they go, and what did they find?

Visitors can explore 80 missions from space agencies around the world and 90 pieces of hardware mapped to their real coordinates. They can also watch three narrated documentaries, walk through a 3D museum, drive a Mars rover, and meet the people behind the missions. Every fact and image links to its source.

Features and how they work

  1. Hardware Locator (main feature). A 3D globe of the Moon and Mars with 90 landers, rovers, instruments, retroreflectors, impact sites and a helicopter, each pinned at its published coordinates. Selecting a pin shows:
    Visitors can filter and compare machines and open each one’s full mission page. A narrated cinematic intro opens the locator, and the homepage has a lighter 2D preview map.
    • the machine’s mission and agency
    • launch and landing dates
    • its coordinates and how accurate they are
    • its condition and whether it still works today (for example, the Apollo retroreflectors are still used for laser ranging)
  2. Documentaries. The site has three narrated documentaries:
    All three have English narration, captions in five languages, a transcript, chapter navigation, keyboard controls and an original music score.
    • The Moon: Humanity’s Journey to Another World. Six chapters, from the first lunar probes through Apollo, Lunokhod and Chandrayaan, ending with the “silent Moon” where these machines still rest. Its theme: “They came. They explored. They were left behind.”
    • Mars: The Journey, the Machines and the Legacy. Seven chapters covering early failed attempts, Mariner and Viking, the rovers, and the future of human exploration. It uses real footage from Mars, orbital images and archival film, and labels every visual as a photo, spacecraft image, animation or artist’s concept.
    • The Silent Legacy. A short film about everything left behind on both worlds, built from NASA archival imagery.
  3. The Humans Behind the Machines. Every machine was built by people, and the site tells their stories in two ways:
    • The Minds Behind the Mission. On each NASA and ESA mission page: the scientists and engineers involved, their role, what they did and why it mattered, each with a link to a biography.
    • The Words That Remain. A searchable collection of real quotes from astronauts and mission teams. Each quote shows its date, mission, context and source, and visitors can filter by mission or sort by date.
  4. 3D Virtual Museum. A walkable 3D hall with real NASA 3D models of the Saturn V, Apollo Lunar Module, Viking lander, Spirit/Opportunity rover, Perseverance and Ingenuity. Visitors walk with the keyboard or touch and can rotate and zoom to inspect any model. Each model links to its mission page, and a text directory appears if a device can’t run 3D.
  5. 3D Mars Rover: The Last Journey. An interactive story of the Opportunity rover. Visitors drive it across Mars and follow its 15-year mission, from landing to the 2018 dust storm and its last data on sol 5,111.
  6. 3D Solar System. A real-time 3D model of the planets with NASA textures. Visitors can rotate and zoom to see where our machines have travelled.
  7. Mission pages, with What Did It Find? Each mission page has:
    • an overview
    • engineering and hardware details
    • its scientific instruments
    • its key discoveries, each explaining why it matters
  8. Moon and Mars pages. Each world has its own page covering every mission that went there, the failures and successes, how each machine’s journey ended, and what comes next.
  9. Why Mars? An explainer on why Mars matters for human exploration, including an interactive cross-section showing where the water is. Each claim is tagged known (measured by missions), tested (shown to work) or proposed (still being studied).
  10. Mission Archive and Timeline. Visitors can search all 80 missions by agency, type, status and decade. The timeline shows every launch since 1957.
  11. International Exploration. Missions from NASA, ESA, the Soviet Union/Roscosmos, ISRO, CNSA, JAXA, the UAE and more, showing that exploration is a shared global story.
  12. Destinations. 13 destinations, from low Earth orbit to interstellar space.
  13. NOVA AI Assistant. A chat guide that answers questions about missions and discoveries. It answers from the site’s own archive first, labels anything that comes from outside it, and can read answers aloud.
  14. Accessibility and reach:
    • five languages: English, Bangla, Spanish, French and Arabic, with full right-to-left layout for Arabic
    • Low Data Mode for slow connections
    • captions and transcripts
    • keyboard navigation and screen-reader labels
    • mobile-first design

Benefits

  • One trusted place. It turns scattered, technical NASA records into one clear, sourced place to learn.
  • Learning by doing. Students find machines on a map, drive a rover, walk through a museum and watch documentaries instead of only reading.
  • People, not just machines. It shows the scientists, engineers and astronauts behind each mission, so careers in space feel real and possible.
  • Open to everyone. It works on low-cost phones, slow internet and in five languages, so learners in countries like Bangladesh can use it as easily as anyone else.
  • Honest science. It shows coordinate accuracy, labels animations and concepts, and separates what is known, tested and proposed.

Intended impact

We want young people to see these machines as part of humanity’s story: our first footprints on other worlds, and the people who put them there. We hope it inspires the next generation of engineers and scientists, especially in countries that are just starting to take part in space exploration. Teachers can use it as a free classroom resource, and anyone can use it to explore space history in their own language.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript (vanilla, with no framework, to keep it fast and light).
  • 3D graphics: Three.js (WebGL) with OrbitControls, and NASA’s official glTF 3D models.
  • Data and media:
    • NASA Image and Video Library
    • NASA, JPL and USGS planetary maps and textures
    • NASA NSSDCA mission records and published landing coordinates
  • AI and audio:
    • NOVA runs through a secure serverless function, so no API key is exposed in the browser.
    • The browser’s Web Speech API reads NOVA’s answers aloud.
    • Narration was created with ElevenLabs.
    • Captions were transcribed from the audio with Whisper speech recognition.
    • The original music score was synthesized with Python.
    • We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant during development.
  • Hosting: Vercel.
  • Testing and production:
    • Playwright for automated testing
    • Google Lighthouse for performance
    • FFmpeg and Python for video and audio processing
  • Typography: Montserrat and DM Mono, with Anek Bangla and IBM Plex Sans Arabic for Bangla and Arabic.

What makes it creative

Most space websites focus on missions. Ours focuses on the machines that stayed behind and the people who built them, and treats each machine as an explorer with a story.

It combines several formats in one connected experience, each suited to a different way of learning:

  • a scientific map
  • three narrated documentaries
  • a walkable 3D museum
  • a rover driving story
  • the people behind the missions
  • an AI guide

A visitor can go from a pin on the map, to what that rover discovered, to the engineers who built it, to the words its team left behind.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: authentic NASA imagery only, nothing made up, a source for every fact, coordinate accuracy shown on the map, and every visual labelled.
  • Audience: clear language for students and casual fans, with depth for anyone who wants more.
  • Accessibility: five languages, right-to-left support, captions, transcripts, keyboard and screen-reader support, and Low Data Mode.
  • Performance: 3D, video and audio load only when needed, so the site runs well on mobile and slow networks.
  • Global fairness: missions from all nations, not just one agency.
  • Security: API keys stay on the server, never in the browser.
  • Respect: these are historic sites and artifacts, and we present them, and the people behind them, with care.
